items.stem: State what is meant by the term "program counter (PC)".
items.answer: The register that holds the memory address of the next instruction to be fetched
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the register that holds the memory address of the next instruction to be fetched. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): The MAR is connected to the address bus.
Reason (R): The MAR holds the address of the memory location to be accessed.
Which option is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: A. Both true; holding the address is why the MAR drives the address bus.

items.stem: A student claims: "The program counter counts how many instructions have been executed so far." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The PC holds the address of the next instruction to fetch; after a jump it can move backwards or forwards, so it is not a count.
items.markingKey: The PC holds the address of the next instruction to fetch; after a jump it can move backwards or forwards, so it is not a count. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Sana hand-traces this accumulator program (address: contents) starting with ACC = 0.
0: LOAD 20
1: ADD 21
2: SUB 22
3: STORE 23
4: HALT
20: 8
21: 2
22: 15
State the value stored at address 23 and the value in the accumulator when the program halts, and the number of fetch-decode-execute cycles completed.
items.answer: Address 23 = -5; ACC = -5; 5 cycles (including HALT)
items.markingKey: Address 23 = -5; ACC = -5; 5 cycles (including HALT). 1 mark for each value.

items.stem:
(a) State what is meant by the term "program counter (PC)". [2]
(b) Explain how the control unit and the ALU work together to execute an ADD instruction. [2]
(c) An image-filter routine executes 20,000,000 instructions with an average of 1.5 clock cycles per instruction on a 3.6 GHz single-core CPU. Calculate the execution time in milliseconds. [3]
items.answer: (a) The register that holds the memory address of the next instruction to be fetched (b) The CU decodes the opcode, then signals memory to fetch the operand into the MDR and signals the ALU to add the MDR to the accumulator; the ALU performs the addition and the result is written back into the accumulator, with status flags updated. (c) 8.333 ms
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] 1 mark for the core idea: the register that holds the memory address of the next instruction to be fetched. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0. (b) [2 marks] Award marks for: The CU decodes the opcode, then signals memory to fetch the operand into the MDR and signals the ALU to add the MDR to the accumulator; the ALU performs the addition and the result is written back into the accumulator, with status flags updated. (one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.) (c) [3 marks] Cycles = 20,000,000 × 1.5 = 30,000,000 (M1); time = cycles ÷ 3.6×10^9 Hz (M1) = 8.333 ms (A1).

items.stem: A benchmark program executes 8,000,000 instructions with an average of 4 clock cycles per instruction on a 2.5 GHz single-core CPU. Calculate the execution time in milliseconds.
Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Adding more registers to a CPU is the most effective way to improve its performance."
items.answer: More registers help, but performance depends on the balance of clock speed, cache, cores and memory bandwidth; registers alone are rarely the most effective change.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: registers are the fastest storage so fewer slow memory accesses are needed; compilers can keep loop variables in registers. Arguments against: registers take die area and add complexity to instruction encoding; clock speed, cache size, pipelining and number of cores often have larger effects; context switches must save and restore more registers. Supported judgement: More registers help, but performance depends on the balance of clock speed, cache, cores and memory bandwidth; registers alone are rarely the most effective change.

items.stem:
Case study context: Kibera Learning Hub, a community school in Nairobi, has a computer lab of 30 thin clients, a small file server and an unreliable internet connection shared by staff and students.
(a) Explain the difference between the address bus and the data bus. Refer to Kibera Learning Hub in your answer. [2]
(b) "Adding more registers to a CPU is the most effective way to improve its performance." Discuss. Refer to Kibera Learning Hub in your answer. [4]
items.answer: (a) The address bus carries memory addresses one way (CPU to memory); the data bus carries the actual data/instructions in both directions between CPU and memory. (b) More registers help, but performance depends on the balance of clock speed, cache, cores and memory bandwidth; registers alone are rarely the most effective change.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] The address bus carries memory addresses one way (CPU to memory); the data bus carries the actual data/instructions in both directions between CPU and memory. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions). (b) [4 marks] Arguments for: registers are the fastest storage so fewer slow memory accesses are needed; compilers can keep loop variables in registers. Arguments against: registers take die area and add complexity to instruction encoding; clock speed, cache size, pipelining and number of cores often have larger effects; context switches must save and restore more registers. Supported judgement: More registers help, but performance depends on the balance of clock speed, cache, cores and memory bandwidth; registers alone are rarely the most effective change. items.stem: Explain how the control unit and the ALU work together to execute an ADD instruction.
items.answer: The CU decodes the opcode, then signals memory to fetch the operand into the MDR and signals the ALU to add the MDR to the accumulator; the ALU performs the addition and the result is written back into the accumulator, with status flags updated.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The CU decodes the opcode, then signals memory to fetch the operand into the MDR and signals the ALU to add the MDR to the accumulator; the ALU performs the addition and the result is written back into the accumulator, with status flags updated. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between the MAR and the MDR.
items.answer: The MAR holds the address of the memory location being accessed; the MDR holds the content (data or instruction) transferred to or from that location.
items.markingKey: The MAR holds the address of the memory location being accessed; the MDR holds the content (data or instruction) transferred to or from that location. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
A simple CPU uses an accumulator. Main memory contains the program and data below (address: contents).
0: LOAD 30
1: ADD 31
2: STORE 33
3: HALT
30: 30
31: 8
32: 14
Execution starts with PC = 0 and ACC = 0. During each fetch MAR ← PC, MDR ← memory[MAR], CIR ← MDR, PC ← PC + 1; during execute the operand address is placed in the MAR and the operand (or, for STORE, the value written) is in the MDR. State the contents of the PC, MAR, MDR and ACC immediately after the instruction at address 2 has been executed.
items.answer: PC = 3, MAR = 33, MDR = 38, ACC = 38
items.markingKey: 1 mark each: PC = 3, MAR = 33, MDR = 38, ACC = 38. (Trace: after 0: ACC=30; after 1: ACC=38; after 2: ACC=38)

items.stem: "The ALU decodes instructions before carrying them out." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Decoding is done by the control unit; the ALU only performs the arithmetic/logic operations it is told to.
items.markingKey: Decoding is done by the control unit; the ALU only performs the arithmetic/logic operations it is told to. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "graphics processing unit (GPU)"?
options: A processor with thousands of simple cores designed to perform the same operation on many data items in parallel, originally for rendering images
The register that holds the data or instruction just read from memory, or about to be written to memory
A form of parallelism in which one instruction is applied to many data items at once
The ability to increase or decrease computing resources quickly to match demand
items.answer: A processor with thousands of simple cores designed to perform the same operation on many data items in parallel, originally for rendering images
items.markingKey: A. "graphics processing unit (GPU)" is a processor with thousands of simple cores designed to perform the same operation on many data items in parallel, originally for rendering images.

items.stem: Explain why CPUs devote much of their chip area to cache and control logic.
items.answer: General-purpose code is sequential and branch-heavy, so large caches reduce memory latency and branch prediction/out-of-order logic keep a single thread running quickly.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: General-purpose code is sequential and branch-heavy, so large caches reduce memory latency and branch prediction/out-of-order logic keep a single thread running quickly. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between latency and throughput.
items.answer: Latency is the time for one task to complete; throughput is the number of tasks completed per unit time. CPUs minimise latency, GPUs maximise throughput.
items.markingKey: Latency is the time for one task to complete; throughput is the number of tasks completed per unit time. CPUs minimise latency, GPUs maximise throughput. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: 50% of a protein-folding calculation can be run in parallel. Using Amdahl's law, calculate the speed-up when it runs on 1024 cores.

A filter needs 200 operations per pixel on a 2560×1440 frame. A CPU has 16 cores each doing 2 × 10^9 operations per second; a GPU has 1024 cores each doing 0.5 × 10^9 operations per second. Assuming perfect parallelism, calculate the time per frame on each and how many times faster the GPU is.
items.answer: CPU 23.04 ms, GPU 1.44 ms; GPU ≈ 16× faster

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "A school should buy GPU workstations rather than CPU-only computers for its computer science lab."
items.answer: Only worthwhile if the curriculum includes ML, graphics or simulation; otherwise CPU computers give better value.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: GPUs accelerate machine-learning projects, rendering and simulations; students gain experience with parallel programming. Arguments against: most programming tasks are sequential and run well on a CPU; GPU workstations cost more and use more power; software may need special frameworks (CUDA) to use the GPU. Supported judgement: Only worthwhile if the curriculum includes ML, graphics or simulation; otherwise CPU computers give better value.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A single chip containing two or more independent processing cores that can execute instructions simultaneously"?
options: run-length encoding (RLE)
cloud computing
multi-core processor
scalability
items.answer: multi-core processor
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of multi-core processor.

items.stem: Leila writes: "A GPU is just a faster CPU, so it could replace the CPU in a laptop." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: GPU cores are simpler and slow at sequential, branching work such as running the OS; the CPU is still needed to control the system and run general code.
items.markingKey: GPU cores are simpler and slow at sequential, branching work such as running the OS; the CPU is still needed to control the system and run general code. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: For each task, state whether a CPU or a GPU is more suitable and justify your choice: (a) training a convolutional neural network on 50 000 images; (b) simulating fluid flow on a grid of 10 million cells; (c) compiling a large Java project.
items.answer: (a) GPU – the work is large matrix multiplications that are data-parallel; (b) GPU – the same update is applied to every cell each time step; (c) CPU – compilation involves complex, branching, mostly sequential work
items.markingKey: 1 mark per correct choice with justification: (a) GPU – the work is large matrix multiplications that are data-parallel; (b) GPU – the same update is applied to every cell each time step; (c) CPU – compilation involves complex, branching, mostly sequential work.

items.stem: What happens when RAM is full and virtual memory is used heavily?
options: Thrashing: the computer slows down because pages are constantly swapped with the disk
The cache becomes non-volatile
The CPU clock speed increases
ROM is used to store programs
items.answer: Thrashing: the computer slows down because pages are constantly swapped with the disk
items.markingKey: A. Disk access is thousands of times slower than RAM.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): RAM is non-volatile.
Reason (R): RAM is used to hold programs that are currently running.
Which option is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
items.answer: A is false but R is true.
items.markingKey: D. A false (RAM is volatile); R true.

items.stem: Explain the difference between SRAM and DRAM.
items.answer: SRAM uses flip-flops, is faster, more expensive and used for cache; DRAM stores bits in capacitors that must be refreshed, is cheaper and denser and used for main memory.
items.markingKey: SRAM uses flip-flops, is faster, more expensive and used for cache; DRAM stores bits in capacitors that must be refreshed, is cheaper and denser and used for main memory. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A cache has an access time of 3 ns and main memory 80 ns; the hit rate is 90%. Assume cache and main memory are searched at the same time, so a miss costs only the main-memory time. Calculate the effective (average) memory access time.
items.markingKey: 0.9 × 3 + 0.1 × 80 (M1) = 10.7 ns (A1). Without cache: 80 ns, so ≈ 7.48× faster.

items.stem: A cache holds 3 blocks and is initially empty. It uses FIFO replacement (the block that has been in the cache longest is evicted). The CPU requests these blocks in order: E E E B B A A D C A E. State the number of hits and misses, the hit rate, and the final contents of the cache.
items.answer: 5 hits, 6 misses, hit rate 45.5%; final cache {C, D, E}
items.markingKey: Sequence of results: M H H M H M H M M H M. 5 hits, 6 misses, hit rate 45.5%; final cache {C, D, E}. 1 mark each for hits/misses, hit rate and final contents; 1 mark for a correct trace.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Upgrading RAM is the most cost-effective way to speed up an old laptop."
items.answer: Only when the laptop regularly runs out of RAM; otherwise replacing a hard disk with an SSD is usually more effective.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: eliminates paging/thrashing if RAM is the bottleneck; cheap compared with a new CPU. Arguments against: no effect if RAM is not full; an SSD may give a bigger improvement for boot and load times; some laptops have soldered RAM. Supported judgement: Only when the laptop regularly runs out of RAM; otherwise replacing a hard disk with an SSD is usually more effective.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "memory hierarchy".
items.answer: The arrangement of storage from small, fast, expensive registers and cache down to large, slow, cheap secondary storage
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the arrangement of storage from small, fast, expensive registers and cache down to large, slow, cheap secondary storage. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why a computer has several levels of cache rather than a single large cache.
items.answer: Small caches can be very fast and close to the core (L1), while larger caches (L2/L3) are slower but hold more; the hierarchy balances speed, cost and hit rate.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Small caches can be very fast and close to the core (L1), while larger caches (L2/L3) are slower but hold more; the hierarchy balances speed, cost and hit rate. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "ROM cannot be changed at all, so firmware updates are impossible." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Modern ROM is flash/EEPROM which can be rewritten (flashed) occasionally, which is how firmware updates are installed.
items.markingKey: Modern ROM is flash/EEPROM which can be rewritten (flashed) occasionally, which is how firmware updates are installed. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Original size divided by compressed size"?

address bus
memory data register (MDR)
virtual memory

items.stem: Distinguish between lossless compression and lossy compression.
items.answer: Lossless compression allows the exact original to be restored (used for text, programs); lossy compression permanently discards some data for much smaller files (used for images, audio, video).
items.markingKey: Lossless compression allows the exact original to be restored (used for text, programs); lossy compression permanently discards some data for much smaller files (used for images, audio, video). items.stem:
Assertion (A): SSDs have faster access times than HDDs.
Reason (R): SSDs have no moving read/write heads.
Which option is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

items.stem: A student claims: "A ZIP file is lossy because it makes the file smaller." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: ZIP uses lossless compression; size reduction alone does not imply data loss.
items.markingKey: ZIP uses lossless compression; size reduction alone does not imply data loss. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A row of pixels in a simple image is stored as the characters YYYGYYGGGGGRRYYYYY (18 characters). Encode it using run-length encoding in the form count followed by colour (e.g. 3W), and state how many characters the encoded form uses.
items.answer: 3Y1G2Y5G2R5Y (12 characters)
items.markingKey: 3Y1G2Y5G2R5Y (12 characters). 1 mark per correct run group (max 2), 1 mark for the count.

items.stem: A photographer in Cape Town must store 2 TB of RAW photos, edit current projects quickly and keep an off-site backup. Recommend a combination of storage devices and compression methods, justifying each choice.
items.answer: SSD (e.g. 1 TB NVMe) for current projects – fast loading of large files; large HDD (4 TB) for the full library – cheap per GB; cloud or tape for off-site backup. RAW files stored losslessly to keep full quality; JPEG (lossy) exports for sharing online because smaller; ZIP/lossless for archives. Justifications must link speed, capacity, cost and data loss.
items.markingKey: SSD (e.g. 1 TB NVMe) for current projects – fast loading of large files; large HDD (4 TB) for the full library – cheap per GB; cloud or tape for off-site backup. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "lossless compression"?
options: The part of the CPU that decodes instructions and sends control signals to coordinate the other components and the flow of data
Compression that reduces file size so that the original data can be reconstructed exactly, e.g. run-length encoding
A cloud model providing virtual machines, storage and networks that the customer configures and manages, including the operating system
Magnetic secondary storage in which a read/write head moves over spinning platters
items.answer: Compression that reduces file size so that the original data can be reconstructed exactly, e.g. run-length encoding
items.markingKey: B. "lossless compression" is compression that reduces file size so that the original data can be reconstructed exactly, e.g. run-length encoding.

items.stem: Explain why SSDs wear out over time.
items.answer: Each flash cell can only be written/erased a limited number of times; wear-levelling spreads writes, but cells eventually fail.

items.answer: 36 MB uncompressed, 3.6 MB compressed; time saved 2.59 s

items.answer: Data may be stored in data centres in other countries with different laws; GDPR requires control over where personal data is processed and how it is protected, so the hospital must ensure the provider complies.

items.stem: A small online shop in Kuala Lumpur currently hosts its website on one server in its office. Discuss whether it should move to IaaS, PaaS or SaaS (an e-commerce platform), considering cost, control, scalability and the skills of its two staff.
items.answer: SaaS e-commerce platform: least technical skill, provider handles security and scaling, monthly fee, limited customisation. PaaS: deploy own code without managing OS, good scaling, needs developer skills. IaaS: most control but staff must manage OS, patches and security. With two non-specialist staff, SaaS (or PaaS if custom features are essential) is most appropriate; on-site server has single point of failure and poor scalability.
items.markingKey: SaaS e-commerce platform: least technical skill, provider handles security and scaling, monthly fee, limited customisation. items.stem: Briefly explain why a company might choose IaaS instead of SaaS.
items.answer: IaaS gives full control over the OS, software and configuration, so the company can run custom or legacy software and meet specific security settings, although it must manage and patch them itself.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: IaaS gives full control over the OS, software and configuration, so the company can run custom or legacy software and meet specific security settings, although it must manage and patch them itself. items.stem:

items.stem: A weather service runs a simulation in which 92% of the work can be parallelised. Compare running it on an 8-core CPU and on a GPU with 2048 cores, using Amdahl's law, and discuss two other factors that affect which processor is better.
items.answer: Speed-up = 1/((1 − p) + p/N): 8 cores → 1/(0.08 + 0.115) ≈ 5.13; 2048 cores → 1/(0.08 + 0.000449) ≈ 12.43, limited by the 8% serial part (max 12.5). Other factors: cost of copying data to GPU memory, whether the code can be written for the GPU, power consumption, memory size; the GPU gives about 2.4× more speed-up but serial code dominates.

items.stem: A CPU has a cache with access time 2 ns and main memory with access time 60 ns. Explain, with a calculation for a hit rate of 95%, why caches dramatically reduce the average memory access time, and discuss why the hit rate can fall.
